worked_solution:
The Wronskian $W({x}_{1},{x}_{2})$ of two vector-valued functions

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{11}(t) \\ {x}_{21}(t)\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{12}(t) \\ {x}_{22}(t)\end{aligned}]
$$

is defined as

$$
W({x}_{1},{x}_{2})=det({x}_{1},{x}_{2})=|\begin{aligned}{x}_{11}(t) & {x}_{12}(t) \\ {x}_{21}(t) & {x}_{22}(t)\end{aligned}|.
$$

Note the following:

- If the Wronskian is not identically zero, then ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are linearly independent.

- If the Wronskian is identically zero, and it's known that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are solutions to the same system of linear ODEs, then ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are linearly dependent. In this case, they do **not** form a fundamental set of solutions.

First, we write our system in matrix form:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]x(t).
$$

Now, let's substitute the given vectors into the matrix differential equation:

- $a(t)=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} \\ {e}^{3t}\end{aligned}]$ $\text{is}$ a solution of the system. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}({e}^{3t})^{′} \\ ({e}^{3t})^{′}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} \\ {e}^{3t}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}3{e}^{3t} \\ 3{e}^{3t}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2\cdot {e}^{3t}+1\cdot {e}^{3t} \\ 1\cdot {e}^{3t}+2\cdot {e}^{3t}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}3{e}^{3t} \\ 3{e}^{3t}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{3t} \\ 3{e}^{3t}\end{aligned}]\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- $b(t)=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{aligned}]$ $\text{isn't}$ a solution of the system. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}({e}^{t})^{′} \\ ({e}^{t})^{′}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2\cdot {e}^{t}+1\cdot {e}^{t} \\ 1\cdot {e}^{t}+2\cdot {e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{t} \\ 3{e}^{t}\end{aligned}]\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- $c(t)=[\begin{aligned}5{e}^{3t} \\ 5{e}^{3t}\end{aligned}]$ $\text{is}$ also a solution of the system. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}(5{e}^{3t})^{′} \\ (5{e}^{3t})^{′}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5{e}^{3t} \\ 5{e}^{3t}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}15{e}^{3t} \\ 15{e}^{3t}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2\cdot 5{e}^{3t}+1\cdot 5{e}^{3t} \\ 1\cdot 5{e}^{3t}+2\cdot 5{e}^{3t}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}15{e}^{3t} \\ 15{e}^{3t}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}15{e}^{3t} \\ 15{e}^{3t}\end{aligned}]\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Now, consider the set of solutions ${a,c}.$ Its Wronskian is

$$
\begin{aligned}W(a,c) & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} & 5{e}^{3t} \\ {e}^{3t} & 5{e}^{3t}\end{aligned}| \\  & =({e}^{3t})(5{e}^{3t})-(5{e}^{3t})({e}^{3t}) \\  & =5{e}^{6t}-5{e}^{6t} \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which is zero for all $t\in R.$ Thus, since $a$ and $c$ are both solutions of the same linear system, but their Wronskian is identically zero, they are linearly dependent and do **not** form a fundamental set of solutions of the system.

The Wronskian W(x1,x2) of two vector-valued functions
x1(t)=[x11(t)x21(t)],x2(t)=[x12(t)x22(t)]
is defined as
W(x1,x2)=det(x1,x2)=|x11(t)x12(t)x21(t)x22(t)|.

Note the following:

  • If the Wronskian is not identically zero, then x1 and x2 are linearly independent.

  • If the Wronskian is identically zero, and it's known that x1 and x2 are solutions to the same system of linear ODEs, then x1 and x2 are linearly dependent. In this case, they do not form a fundamental set of solutions.

First, we write our system in matrix form:

x′(t)=[2112]x(t).

Now, let's substitute the given vectors into the matrix differential equation:

  • a(t)=[e3te3t] is a solution of the system. Indeed:
    [(e3t)′(e3t)′]=[2112][e3te3t][3e3t3e3t]=[2⋅e3t+1⋅e3t1⋅e3t+2⋅e3t][3e3t3e3t]=[3e3t3e3t]✓

  • b(t)=[etet] isn't a solution of the system. Indeed:
    [(et)′(et)′]=[2112][etet][etet]=[2⋅et+1⋅et1⋅et+2⋅et][etet]=[3et3et]×

  • c(t)=[5e3t5e3t] is also a solution of the system. Indeed:
    [(5e3t)′(5e3t)′]=[2112][5e3t5e3t][15e3t15e3t]=[2⋅5e3t+1⋅5e3t1⋅5e3t+2⋅5e3t][15e3t15e3t]=[15e3t15e3t]✓

Now, consider the set of solutions {a,c}. Its Wronskian is

W(a,c)=|e3t5e3te3t5e3t|=(e3t)(5e3t)−(5e3t)(e3t)=5e6t−5e6t=0,

which is zero for all t∈R. Thus, since a and c are both solutions of the same linear system, but their Wronskian is identically zero, they are linearly dependent and do not form a fundamental set of solutions of the system.
